items.headline: Jury convicts Huawei of fraud and conspiracy
items.summary: A federal jury in New York found Chinese tech giant Huawei guilty of conspiring to steal trade secrets and of bank fraud, in a case that also involved its business with Iran. The verdict caps a long-running U.S. prosecution of the company.

items.headline: Report says Trump may have profited from Huang's return
items.summary: A new report suggests President Trump may have gained millions of dollars after he intervened to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive. The findings add to questions about the president's financial stake in the chipmaker.

items.headline: Abrego Garcia leaves U.S. for Spain
items.summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran immigrant who became a symbol of the administration's deportation campaign, left the United States voluntarily for Spain. His departure follows nearly two years of legal battles.

items.headline: China investigates Shanghai party chief Chen Jining
items.summary: Chinese authorities opened an investigation into Politburo member and Shanghai Communist Party chief Chen Jining. He is the latest senior official targeted in Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign.

items.headline: Trump to give Giuliani the Medal of Freedom
items.summary: President Trump will award the Presidential Medal of Freedom to Rudy Giuliani, the former New York mayor and his former personal lawyer. Giuliani was a central figure in efforts to overturn the 2020 election result.

items.headline: Legal immigrants lose Medicaid coverage
items.summary: Hundreds of thousands of immigrants living in the U.S. legally have lost Medicaid coverage under a provision of President Trump's tax and spending law. The law is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending.

items.headline: Australia moves to fine tech giants over online harms
items.summary: Australia's government reached a political deal on online safety laws that could impose multibillion-dollar fines on platforms that fail to prevent foreseeable harms. The 'digital duty of care' would put new obligations on large tech companies.

items.headline: Probe into forged titles clouds Kushner's Albania project
items.summary: Albania's prime minister says Jared Kushner's planned resort will go ahead as planned. But a state prosecutor's investigation into forged land titles could halt the development.

items.headline: Experts weigh fallout of failed climate talks
items.summary: Dozens of nations objected to the U.N. climate summit's final text because it did not mention fossil fuels or raise financial help for poorer countries. Experts say the breakdown could deepen inequality but that climate progress has not stalled.

items.headline: Taipei candidate on countering Chinese influence
items.summary: Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen spoke with TIME about fighting what he calls Chinese cognitive warfare. The interview comes as Taiwan weighs how to resist pressure from Beijing.

digest.overview:
A New York jury convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 criminal counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud. A new report suggests President Trump may have profited by millions after he pushed Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang, and Trump said he would pardon Huang if needed. The administration is preparing higher tariffs on China, the EU and 14 other trading partners, with China facing duties of up to 20%. Kilmar Abrego Garcia left the country voluntarily for Spain after nearly two years of legal fights. Trump will award Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Hundreds of thousands of legal immigrants have lost Medicaid under the president's tax law, and states sued HUD over a rule ending housing aid for mixed-status families. Record king tides threaten flooding along the West Coast.

Abroad, Yemen's Houthis struck Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund headquarters for the second time in a week, injuring 11, and Iran said it shot down two U.S. drones near the Strait of Hormuz. Russia attacked Naftogaz gas facilities in Ukraine's Poltava region, while a Ukrainian drone strike cut power in Russia's Samara region. China opened an investigation into Shanghai party chief Chen Jining and launched Shenzhou-24 carrying a Pakistani astronaut. Australia struck a deal on online safety laws with multibillion-dollar fines for tech firms. In France, Nicolas Sarkozy was ordered to stand trial over an alleged witness-tampering scheme. Malaysia plans to send 6,803 migrants and refugees back to Myanmar next month.

fact.answer:
When a plane climbs or descends, outside air pressure changes, but air sealed in your middle ear doesn't adjust on its own, so the mismatch pushes or pulls on the eardrum. Relief comes through the Eustachian tube, a narrow passage from the middle ear to the back of the nose; when it opens, the pressure evens out, and that opening is the "pop."

The tube normally stays closed until swallowing or yawning pulls it open. Takeoff is usually easier, since middle-ear air can push its way out; on landing, higher outside pressure presses in and is harder to relieve.

Chewing gum, swallowing or yawning during descent helps; babies can be fed or given a pacifier. If a cold blocks the tube, the pressure can't equalize, and it can hurt a lot.
fact.question: Why do your ears pop on an airplane?
